title: Cautions
hook: teachers warn against magic, charms sold for money, and study without grounding

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavanot: intentions attached to the words of prayer. Your line was intend. Which blessing or thank-you did you mean on purpose? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

A charm in a shop window, with Hebrew letters stamped on it and a little card promising luck. A course online that says it will unlock the secret names in a weekend, card details please. The word Kabbalah can end up on a price tag. That can make the whole subject look like a sales pitch. But some of the sharpest warnings about this kind of thing don't come from critics outside. They come from inside the tradition, from the Torah, the Mishnah and its own teachers. Today's word.
screen: `A CHARM WITH A PRICE TAG.` → `SECRETS IN A WEEKEND.` → `THE WARNINGS COME FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Cautions. Turn them four ways. First, the Torah's own line. Deuteronomy names practices that are not to be found among the people: divining, reading omens, sorcery, casting spells, asking the dead. Then it sums up what it wants instead, in a short phrase that begins tamim tihyeh: be whole-hearted with the LORD your God. Not clever, not powerful. Whole. Second, the crown and the spade. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Tzadok says not to make the Torah a crown to make yourself great, nor a spade to dig with. Holy learning isn't a tool for status or a way to dig up money. Charms sold for profit fall right under that warning. Third, words as cures. Maimonides objected to people who whisper over a wound and read a verse of Torah to heal it. The words of Torah, he wrote, are healing for the soul, not medicine for the body. And within Kabbalah itself, teachers drew a line between learning about God and trying to use holy names to change things in the world, and warned students away from the second. Fourth, grounding. Mystical ideas without a floor under them can drift: into fear, into pride, into the feeling of having secret knowledge others don't. The tradition's answer is a floor of plain learning, a community, and a teacher whose life matches their words. So study carefully looks like ordinary questions. Who taught this person? What do they ask of me? Does this teaching send me back toward kindness, honest work and the commandments, or toward my wallet? A careful student isn't a suspicious one. They just check the ground before they stand on it.
screen: `BE WHOLE-HEARTED, NOT POWERFUL.` · `NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.` · `VERSES HEAL THE SOUL.` · `A FLOOR UNDER THE MYSTERY.` · then, large: `STUDY CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from a reliable source. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've picked up lately about faith, or about yourself: a post, a video, a quote, a piece of advice. Hold it up to the light. Where did it come from? Who taught the person who said it? Did it ask you for money, or fear, or nothing at all? No need to throw it away. Just notice how firm its ground is. Then bring to mind one source you trust more deeply: a teacher, a book, a person whose life matches their words. Rest with them. The bell holds the time.
Cautions. The tradition's own warnings: no magic, no selling holy things, and no mystical study without solid ground beneath it. Today's word.
Your line: study carefully. Today, before you share or believe one thing you read about faith, look for who first said it, and who taught them. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish mysticism is traditionally studied within a framework of Torah, Jewish law and community, and teachers in the tradition warn students away from amulets, paid blessings and the use of holy names as magic.
